pipeline_name: High Island Offshore Gas Pipeline System

validity.recommendation: no edit needed; existence, ownership, and classification are solidly documented
validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: solidly real. Proposed Sept 1975 by 5 partners (American Natural Gas, United Gas Pipe Line, Texas Gas Transmission, Natural Gas Pipeline Co. of America, Transco), construction began Aug 1 1976, in service early 1978 -- corroborated by two independent, decades-apart sources: offshore-mag.com (2018 retrospective) and Oil & Gas Journal via TRID/TRB abstract (Ewing, R.C., 'High Island Offshore System's Pipeline Network Under Way in Gulf,' OGJ 75(2), Jan 1977) -- the two agree on diameter breakdown (67mi 42in / 26mi 36in / 110.5mi 30in) and capacity (988 MMcf/d initial, expandable to 2 bcf/d). CLASSIFICATION: 'both transmission and gathering' is correct -- a 2009 PHMSA (DOT) pipeline-safety interpretation letter (reposted at viadata.wordpress.com) states FERC and PHMSA agree certain HIOS portions are gathering while the segment interconnecting with UTOS is transmission. DUPLICATE: NOT a duplicate of P0188 UTOS -- the same PHMSA letter independently states UTOS is a distinct 29-mile, 42-inch line that receives 'wet gas' from HIOS at West Cameron Block 167, matching P0188's own roster spec (len=29.0 dia=42) -- two interconnected but physically separate systems, not a double-count. OWNERSHIP: Genesis Energy, L.P., 100%, confirmed by TWO independent sources -- Genesis's own current operations page ('Genesis Ownership: 100%') and the third-party pipeline database Rextag ('Owner: Genesis Energy, LP'). Genesis's 2015 $1.5B acquisition of Enterprise's GOM offshore pipeline business is independently reported (Bloomberg, Maritime Executive, Offshore Technology, The Advocate) but those articles name only the OIL systems acquired (Poseidon, SEKCO, CHOPS) -- HIOS is not named in that coverage, so the acquisition articles do not independently corroborate HIOS specifically; ownership rests on Genesis's own site + Rextag's current listing. CAVEAT -- length migration over time: the ORIGINAL 1976-78 construction totaled 203.5 mi (67+26+110.5, per both historical sources); Genesis's CURRENT page instead describes a 152-mile 'core' HIOS plus an 86-mile East Breaks Gathering System addition, totaling 238 mi -- the SAME total the sheet already carries, but not the same physical inventory as the original 203.5 mi (implying some original mainline was retired/re-scoped while the East Breaks Gathering extension was added later). This is consistent with 'the likeliest to have partial abandonments' guidance for this row; I found no dedicated abandonment order for the ORIGINAL mainline itself (see the separate FERC-docket note in status_reviews).

validity.recommendation: drop the BOEM 2008-038.pdf URL from PipelineType [ref] -- it documents an unrelated pipeline; keep only the viadata.wordpress.com PHMSA letter
validity.researcher_notes: The recorded PipelineType [ref] cites two URLs. https://www.boem.gov/sites/default/files/boem-newsroom/Library/Publications/2008/2008-038.pdf resolves (200) and even fuzzy-matches on 'High Island' via url_verifier's --name check, but reading the PDF shows it is a 2008 BOEM/MMS INVESTIGATION REPORT into a 2007 crude-OIL pipeline rupture on the 'High Island Pipeline System' (HIPS), operated at the time by Plains -- a different, oil-gathering system near the same field area, not this gas transmission/gathering row (HIOS). This is a false-positive relevance match (same 'High Island' place name, different pipeline entirely) -- it does not support this row's PipelineType and should not remain in the ref cell. The second URL, https://viadata.wordpress.com/2011/06/10/offshore-gathering-and-transmission-new-interpretation/, IS the correct, on-point source (a 2009 PHMSA pipeline-safety interpretation letter that names HIOS specifically and states FERC agrees parts of HIOS are gathering, parts are transmission) -- keep it alone.

validity.recommendation: reconcile against FERC's Part 284 Informational Postings for HIOS before treating either figure as final
validity.researcher_notes: Third-party pipeline database Rextag (rextag.com/pages/high-island-offshore-system, live 2026, sourced from FERC gas Informational Postings, labeled '(Unofficial)') lists 'Miles of Pipeline: 287' and 'System Capacity: 1.8 Bcf/d' for HIOS -- both DISAGREE with the sheet's recorded LengthKnown=238.00 mi and Capacity=2000.00 MMcf/d. The recorded values are directly supported by Genesis Energy's own current operations page (238 = 152 core + 86 East Breaks Gathering) and by the historical construction/nameplate figures (988 MMcf/d initial, expandable to 2 bcf/d ultimate, per offshore-mag and the 1977 Oil & Gas Journal/TRID article), so I am NOT overriding the recorded values -- Genesis's own direct statement outweighs a third-party aggregator explicitly labeled unofficial. But a 49-mile and 200-MMcf/d gap is material and unexplained; it could reflect additional laterals/platforms Genesis's summary page does not itemize, or a currently-authorized (vs. nameplate-ultimate) capacity. Flagging for a FERC Informational Postings pull (Part 284) as the decisive source, which I did not complete in the time available for this row.

validity.recommendation: review the §8 route geometry against BOEM pipeline-segment records before treating it as an accurate HIOS trace
validity.researcher_notes: The routes-repo geometry (../GOIT-GGIT-pipeline-routes/data/individual-routes/gas-pipelines/P0200.geojson) is a single feature (Operator='High Island Offshore', Count_=38) but its MultiLineString has 60 disconnected parts / 169 vertices spanning roughly 27.87N-29.40N, 94.43W-93.44W. Summing straight-line vertex-to-vertex distance gives ~326 mi, which is longer than BOTH the sheet's 238 mi and Rextag's 287 mi. I did not have per-segment status/size attributes for this dataset (unlike P0256 Stingray's route in this same batch, which carries BOEM STATUS_COD/PPL_SIZE_C fields), so I cannot tell whether some of the 60 parts are abandoned/removed segments folded into this operator-name filter, matching the pattern flagged for Stingray. Given HIOS is independently confirmed as one of the offshore rows most likely to carry partial abandonments (see status_reviews), this geometry is worth a closer BOEM-record check before relying on it for a §8 route candidate.
